module_title: General Veterinary Pathology – Etiology and Classification of Disease
learning_goal: Understand why animals become diseased and classify the causes of disease.
beginner_rule: Never assume prior knowledge of pathology terminology. Introduce a simple idea first, then give the technical term. Do not test a technical term before explaining it.
response_style: Keep teaching brief, interactive and veterinary-focused. Use one main question at a time. Give immediate feedback and a short explanation after every answer.

sessions.title: Session 1 of 8 — Why Does an Animal Become Sick?
sessions.intro: Let's begin with one simple question: WHY does an animal become sick?
sessions.scenario: A healthy calf suddenly develops fever and becomes dull. A veterinarian wants to know what caused this change.
sessions.question: What is the veterinarian trying to find out?
options: A) The cause of the disease
B) The colour of the calf
C) The name of the treatment
D) The breed of the veterinarian
sessions.feedback_correct: Correct! We are trying to find the CAUSE of the disease.
sessions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the question: 'Why did the calf become sick?' We are looking for the cause.
sessions.answer_note: The cause explains why the animal became diseased. The study of disease causes is called etiology.
sessions.veterinary_example: Finding out whether a dog's illness was caused by infection, poisoning, trauma, or another factor.
sessions.remember: Etiology asks: WHY did the animal become sick?

term_card.meaning: The study of the cause or causes of disease.
term_card.example: Finding out why a dog became diseased.

sessions.teaching_point: Etiology is concerned with the cause or causes of disease.
sessions.recap: Etiology asks WHY an animal became sick.

sessions.title: Session 2 of 8 — Predisposing Causes
sessions.intro: Sometimes two animals face a similar situation, but one is more likely to become diseased. Why?
sessions.scenario: Two cattle are exposed to strong sunlight. A white-faced Hereford develops a sun-related lesion around the eye, while a heavily pigmented animal does not.
sessions.question: Which factor could make one animal more susceptible?
sessions.feedback_correct: Correct! Certain characteristics can make an animal more susceptible to disease. These are called predisposing causes.
sessions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the difference between the animals. Their breed and pigmentation can influence susceptibility.
sessions.answer_note: A predisposing cause increases an animal's susceptibility. It does not necessarily produce the disease by itself.
sessions.veterinary_example: Poor pigmentation around the eyelids can increase susceptibility to sun-related lesions in some cattle.
sessions.remember: Predisposing = makes the animal more susceptible.

term_card.meaning: A factor that makes an animal more likely or susceptible to disease.
term_card.example: Breed, age, sex, heredity, species, or pigmentation may increase susceptibility.

sessions.recap: Predisposing causes make an animal more susceptible to disease.

sessions.title: Session 3 of 8 — Definitive Causes: Physical
sessions.intro: Now let's look at factors that can directly produce disease or injury.
sessions.scenario: A dog is hit by a vehicle and develops a fractured limb.
sessions.question: What type of cause directly produced the dog's injury?
sessions.feedback_correct: Correct! A mechanical force from the accident directly produced the injury.
sessions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what physically acted on the dog. It was a mechanical force.
sessions.answer_note: A physical cause is a harmful physical force or energy that produces disease or injury.
sessions.veterinary_example: A dog injured by mechanical trauma during a road accident.
sessions.remember: Physical causes include trauma, heat, cold and radiation.

term_card.meaning: A harmful physical force, energy, temperature or radiation that can produce disease or injury.
term_card.example: Mechanical trauma in a dog after a road accident.

sessions.recap: Physical causes include mechanical trauma, heat, cold and radiation.

sessions.title: Session 4 of 8 — Chemical Causes and Toxins
sessions.intro: Animals may also become diseased after exposure to harmful chemicals or toxic substances.
sessions.scenario: Several sheep become ill after grazing in an area contaminated with an agricultural pesticide.
sessions.question: How should this cause be classified?
sessions.feedback_correct: Correct! A pesticide is a chemical substance that can produce toxicity.
sessions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the clue: the sheep were exposed to a pesticide. That points to a chemical or toxic cause.
sessions.answer_note: Chemical causes are harmful chemical substances. Toxins are harmful substances produced by organisms or occurring naturally in certain sources.
sessions.remember: Chemical / toxic causes can directly produce disease.

term_card.meaning: A harmful chemical substance capable of producing disease or injury.

toxin_examples: Zootoxins – toxins associated with animals, such as snake venom
sessions.recap: Chemical causes and toxins can directly produce disease.

sessions.title: Session 5 of 8 — Biological Causes: Microbial Agents
sessions.intro: Now ask: WHO caused the disease? Many diseases are caused by biological agents.
sessions.scenario: A group of cattle develops fever and characteristic disease after exposure to an infectious agent.
sessions.question: Which of the following is a biological cause of disease?
sessions.feedback_correct: Correct! Bacteria are biological agents capable of causing infectious disease.
sessions.feedback_incorrect: Think about which option is an organism rather than a physical or nutritional factor.
sessions.answer_note: Biological causes include disease-causing organisms and infectious agents.
sessions.veterinary_example: Bacillus anthracis causes anthrax in susceptible animals.
sessions.remember: Microbial biological causes include bacteria, viruses, fungi, mycoplasma and rickettsial organisms.

term_card.meaning: A disease-causing organism or infectious biological agent.

veterinary_examples: Fungi – dermatophytosis in cattle, dogs or cats
sessions.recap: Microbial biological causes include bacteria, viruses, fungi, mycoplasma and rickettsial organisms.

sessions.title: Session 6 of 8 — Biological Causes: Parasites
sessions.intro: Some biological causes are parasites. Let's see how they fit into the classification.
sessions.scenario: A group of goats becomes weak and pale because of a heavy Haemonchus infection.
sessions.question: Haemonchus belongs to which broad group?
sessions.feedback_correct: Correct! Haemonchus is a parasitic organism, so it is a biological cause.
sessions.feedback_incorrect: Haemonchus is a parasite. Parasites belong under biological causes.
sessions.answer_note: Parasitic causes are biological causes. They include protozoa, helminths and arthropods.
sessions.veterinary_example: Haemonchus infection causing disease in sheep or goats.
veterinary_examples: Protozoa – Babesia causing babesiosis in cattle or dogs
Helminths – Haemonchus in sheep and goats
Trematodes – Fasciola causing fasciolosis in cattle
Cestodes – Taenia species causing infection in dogs
Arthropods – ticks affecting cattle and dogs
sessions.recap: Parasitic causes are biological causes and include protozoa, helminths and arthropods.

sessions.title: Session 7 of 8 — Nutritional, Immunological and Miscellaneous Causes
sessions.intro: A few important causes remain. Let's identify them from veterinary situations.
sessions.scenario: A high-producing dairy cow becomes weak and unable to stand shortly after calving. Blood calcium concentration is very low.
sessions.question: Which type of cause should you consider?
sessions.feedback_correct: Correct! Low calcium is a nutritional imbalance associated with milk fever around calving.
sessions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the clue: the cow has very low calcium. Calcium is a nutrient.
sessions.answer_note: Nutritional causes include deficiency, excess or imbalance of nutrients.
sessions.veterinary_example: Milk fever in a dairy cow associated with low blood calcium around calving.
sessions.remember: Nutritional → deficiency or excess. Other remaining groups include immunological and miscellaneous causes.

term_card.meaning: Disease caused by deficiency, excess or imbalance of a nutrient.
term_card.example: Milk fever associated with low calcium in a dairy cow.

additional_examples: Calcium imbalance around calving – milk fever
Iatrogenic – unintended condition associated with veterinary intervention
Idiosyncrasy – unusual individual reaction to a drug or substance
sessions.recap: The remaining definitive causes include nutritional, immunological and miscellaneous causes.

sessions.title: Session 8 of 8 — You Are the Pathologist!
sessions.intro: This is your final challenge. You now have to classify the cause from short veterinary situations.
sessions.scenario: A dog develops injury after being hit by a vehicle.
sessions.question: How should the cause be classified?
sessions.feedback_correct: Excellent! You correctly connected the veterinary situation with the complete classification.
sessions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what directly acted on the dog. It was a physical mechanical force.
sessions.answer_note: A road accident produces mechanical trauma, which is a physical definitive cause.
sessions.veterinary_example: A dog injured by mechanical trauma in a road accident.
sessions.remember: Think: Predisposing factors increase susceptibility; definitive causes actually produce disease or injury.

term_card.meaning: The actual agent or factor that directly produces disease or injury.
term_card.example: Mechanical trauma from a road accident.

challenge_questions.question: A sheep develops disease after eating a poisonous plant. Which category?
challenge_questions.answer_note: A harmful substance from a plant is a phytotoxin and is classified under chemical/toxic causes.

challenge_questions.question: A cow develops fasciolosis due to Fasciola infection. Which category?
challenge_questions.answer_note: Fasciola is a trematode parasite, so it is a biological cause.

challenge_questions.question: A particular breed of dog is more susceptible to a disease. Which category?
challenge_questions.answer_note: Breed is a predisposing factor because it can increase susceptibility.

challenge_questions.question: A cow develops milk fever associated with low blood calcium after calving. Which category?
challenge_questions.answer_note: Low calcium represents a nutritional imbalance.

challenge_questions.question: An animal develops an unintended condition following veterinary intervention. Which category?
challenge_questions.answer_note: Iatrogenic means an unintended condition associated with medical or veterinary intervention.

final_take_home: ETIOLOGY asks: WHY did the animal become sick?
PREDISPOSING causes make an animal more susceptible.
DEFINITIVE causes are the actual agents or factors producing disease or injury.
Definitive causes include physical, chemical/toxic, biological, nutritional, immunological and miscellaneous causes.
sessions.module_complete_message: 🎉 Congratulations! You have completed the Etiology and Classification module. You have moved from asking 'Why did this animal become sick?' to classifying the possible causes like a beginning veterinary pathologist.
